passages.text: I will begin with Zeus himself, the most royal of all. His father Cronus, by swallowing his own children, as you say, and harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern of reverence toward parents and love toward children. Zeus himself bound his own father and imprisoned him in Tartarus, and he punishes the other gods. For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant. To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede. Coming to the aid of adulterers on behalf of adultery, he himself is often found to be an adulterer. He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters Hera, Demeter, and heavenly Aphrodite, whom some call Didone. For those who wish to have relations with daughters, he becomes an evil example from the myths by having had relations with Persephone. Indeed, he has committed countless acts of impiety, so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ βασιλικωτάτου Διὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: with Zeus himself, the most royal of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative describes Zeus as supremely kingly or royal. The rendering preserves its degree rather than replacing it with an unexpressed formal title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἅρπῃ τοῦ πατρὸς Οὐρανοῦ τὰ μόρια θερίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle
lexical_decisions.rationale: The harvesting verb and sickle image are retained, while private parts follows the source's euphemistic noun in this context. Adamant denotes the mythic hard material; steel or diamond would be more specific than the supplied wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς τὰ μυστικὰ τῶν θεῶν ζηλοῦσιν τὸν ὑπογραμμὸν ἔδειξεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can denote mysteries, secret rites, or secret practices, and the verb can express zeal for or emulation of them. The main text retains the mysteries language without deciding whether specific initiation rites are intended. The favorable-sounding pattern of filial reverence and parental love is preserved as the speaker's irony, not replaced by an explanatory moral label.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ ἀρρητουργεῖν θέλουσιν τὴν Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν· ἦν δὲ ἡ Μῆτις γονή· βρέφος γὰρ καταπιεῖν ἀδύνατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active participle explicitly says begot, not impregnated. Γονή can refer to reproductive seed, generation, or offspring; semen best fits the stated contrast with an infant and the surrounding accusation. This preserves the ancient speaker's explanation without substituting a more familiar myth or adding physical detail.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὲρ δὲ ἀπολογίας παιδεραστῶν Γανυμήδην ἁρπάζει
lexical_decisions.chosen: To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase states the apologetic purpose attributed to the mythic act. Lovers of boys renders the historical sexual category without embellishment, and abducts retains the force of seizing or carrying off.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀδελφοφθορεῖν δὲ προτρέπει ἀδελφαῖς συνελθών
lexical_decisions.chosen: He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound verb carries a morally condemnatory sexual sense, while the participle supplies Zeus's own conduct as the inducement. Sexual corruption of sisters is a more literal alternative; the rendering does not specify coercion where the verb alone does not establish it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἣν τινες Διδώνην λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whom some call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed name is transliterated as Didone. It is not silently changed to Dione or equated with Dido on the basis of a more familiar name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵν’ ὑπὸ τῶν δυσσεβῶν διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν ἀκρασίαν θεὸς εἶναι τὸ μύσος δογματισθῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contemptuous neuter noun calls Zeus an abomination. The purpose construction and the stated reason for treating him as divine are retained as the speaker's polemical claim, rather than recast as a neutral statement about Greek belief.

passages.text: You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs. But as for those whose starting point is education, what can one even say? Some of them claim to be grammarians and sophists and affirm that such acts are worthy of gods. For, lacking self-control themselves, they seize on this mythical pretext and are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἰδιώταις ἔχοις περὶ τῶν τοιούτων ὑπολήψεων ἀγανακτεῖν μετρίως εὔλογον
lexical_decisions.chosen: You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs
lexical_decisions.rationale: The potential expression and moderate degree of indignation are both retained. Ἰδιῶται can mean ordinary people or non-specialists; the contrast with the educated supports uneducated here without implying a lack of intelligence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γραμματικοὶ καὶ σοφισταὶ ἀξιοῦντες εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: claim to be grammarians and sophists
lexical_decisions.rationale: The claim to professional learned status is retained. Grammarians here are literary-language scholars as well as teachers of grammar; sophists denotes the historical learned profession rather than simply deceptive arguers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τοιαύτας πράξεις θεῶν ἀξίας. εἶναι βεβαιοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: affirm that such acts are worthy of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construction is read across the printed punctuation: acts is the subject of being worthy, and affirm is the governing verb. No surviving wording is omitted or a missing clause supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς δὴ μιμηταὶ τῶν κρειττόνων ἄσεμνα διαπραττόμενοι παρρησιάζονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses confident openness or boldness, here accompanying conduct. Speak freely is a more speech-specific alternative. The qualification supposedly reflects ὡς δή, and the superior beings are not renamed in the main text where this clause leaves them implicit.

passages.text: For this reason, those who live in the countryside sin much less than they do. They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously. For those who learn their letters through such myths from childhood, while their souls are still tender, ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds. As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul. Worst of all, these deeply rooted acts of impiety cannot even be cut out easily when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful. For everyone delights in remaining in the things to which they have been accustomed from childhood. Thus, since habit has almost as much power as nature, it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ εἰσηγμένοι πονηρῶς δι’ ὧν εἰσήχθησαν οἱ ταῦτα τολμῶντες, ἐκ παιδείας κακῆς ἀσεβεῖν μεμαθηκότες
lexical_decisions.chosen: They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The countryside dwellers are contrasted with those who dare the acts, and the final learned participle describes the latter. The repeated verb of introduction is rendered consistently as instruction; initiation is possible, but need not imply formal mystery initiation in this educational context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν ἀσεβεῖς πράξεις εἰς τὸν αὑτῶν συνφύουσι νοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb depicts the deeds growing together with or into the learner's mind. Ingrain conveys deep incorporation, while the following English retains the explicit seed, fruit, and root images. A more literal alternative is cause the deeds to grow into their own minds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν ἐπαυξηθείσης τῆς ἡλικίας ὡς κακὰ σπέρματα καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ τελεσφοροῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preceding impious deeds supply the contextually inferred subject of bear fruit, with seeds as the explicit comparison. The learners' increasing age is retained. An alternative foregrounds the learners as producing the fruit, but the seed comparison favors the ingrained deeds as what comes to fruition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπόταν ἀνδρωθεῖσιν αὐτοῖς χαλεπὰ εἶναι νοῆται
lexical_decisions.chosen: when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The impious practices remain the things recognized, and the grown men the persons doing the recognizing. Grievous or troublesome is a material alternative to harmful for χαλεπά. The main rendering does not turn this into recognition merely that uprooting the practices is difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς συνηθείας οὐ πολὺ ἔλαττον πρὸς τὴν φύσιν δυναμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: since habit has almost as much power as nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source says habit's power is not much less than nature's, rather than identical to it or greater. Almost as much preserves that comparison in accessible English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσμετάβλητοι γίνονται πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αὐτοῖς καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ καλά
lexical_decisions.chosen: it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their resistance concerns a change toward goods not planted from the outset. The rendering retains the direction of change and the planting image without claiming that such change is impossible.

passages.text: Therefore, young people should not be trained in corrupting lessons, and those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology. For their teachings are far worse than ignorance, as we demonstrated from those who live in the countryside, who sin less because they have not been educated in Greek teachings. One must therefore avoid their myths of this kind, their theaters, and their books—if only it were possible, their cities too. For they are full of evil teachings and breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates; they pass on to those nearby what they themselves have suffered. Worst of all, whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς ὄντας ἐπιμελῶς ὑποστέλλεσθαι τῆς Ἑλλήνων ἐπακούειν μυθολογίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology
lexical_decisions.rationale: Those at their prime are distinguished from the young people just mentioned. Refrain preserves the caution or withdrawal expressed by the middle verb without adding an external enforcer or extending the statement to all Greek learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴθε δυνατὸν ἦν καὶ τὰς πόλεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: if only it were possible, their cities too
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is a wish that avoiding even the cities were possible, not an unqualified claim that it is possible. Avoid is understood from the preceding obligation and is not repeated in Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πνέοντες τοῖς συναμιλλωμένοις ὥσπερ λύσσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates
lexical_decisions.rationale: The breath and contagion-like comparison are retained. Λύσσα can mean raging madness or rabies; frenzy avoids specifying a medical condition, while what is like preserves ὥσπερ rather than making the comparison a literal diagnosis.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅστις παρ’ αὐτοῖς πλεῖον πεπαίδευται, πολλῷ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν οὗτος φρονεῖν ἐκτέτραπται
lexical_decisions.chosen: whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The greater extent of education and the great extent of deviation are both retained, without turning them into a precise proportional scale. The measure is the speaker's thinking in accordance with nature, not an added claim about a particular modern concept of normality.

passages.text: Some among them, even claiming to be philosophers, treat such sins as morally indifferent and call those who are angry at such acts foolish. For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning because those men knew that people, with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another. For these reasons, the wise men established a law and prohibited such acts as sins. But it is ridiculous to think this way. For how are things that cause disturbances, murders, and every kind of turmoil not sins? Do not defrauding people of their livelihoods, the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship, and many other evils arise from adultery?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τοιαῦτα ἁμαρτήματα ἀδιάφορα τίθενται
lexical_decisions.chosen: treat such sins as morally indifferent
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifferent is used in the philosophical sense of neither morally good nor morally bad, not a lack of emotional interest. The speaker's own description of the acts as sins is retained even though the reported philosophers deny that description by nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν (φασί) τὰ τοιαῦτα τῇ φύσει ἁμαρτήματα, ὅσα θετοῖς ἀπηγόρευται νόμοις ὑπὸ τῶν κατ’ ἀρχὰς γενομένων σοφῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative description identifies the acts prohibited by established law, contrasting enacted law with nature. The colon divides the long construction for English readability without changing the prohibition into a natural one. Those in the beginning is retained without specifying a historical period or identifying particular lawmakers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὐριπίστῳ ψυχῇ ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις μεγάλως ἀχθόμενοι πρὸς ἀλλήλους πόλεμον αἴρονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes a soul readily tossed or shifted about; fickle or unstable are material alternatives. The rendering preserves both the strong distress and the resulting interpersonal warfare rather than treating the claim as merely disagreement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: βίων περιγραφαί
lexical_decisions.chosen: defrauding people of their livelihoods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Βίος can denote livelihood or property as well as life, and περιγραφή can denote fraudulent deprivation. The economic sense fits the ensuing household ruin and hardship. Cutting short of lives or loss of property are material alternatives if life or possessions, respectively, are foregrounded. The main text does not add a specific legal or financial mechanism.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἴκων ἀναστάσεις, μαγεῖαι, δόλοι, ἀπορίαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source lists the overturning of households, magical practices, deception, and want or difficulty. Hardship preserves the breadth of ἀπορίαι rather than restricting it to financial destitution; household ruin preserves the destructive force of ἀναστάσεις.
